title: Attacking The Scandi Kingside | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: It's a Scandinavian, just dressed up with an early a6 — not that bad, but our strategy doesn't change. We capture and treat it like a normal Scandi.
With the d-pawn already advanced we simply develop the knight to c3, gaining a tempo on the exposed queen — exactly as in the main Scandinavian.
One subtlety: Black's idea may be b5. You can always meet b5 with a4, softening the queenside pawns — or develop the bishop to c4 first, before b5 ever arrives.
The bishop to c4 develops and lays a trap: if Black grabs space with b5, there's a crushing tactic waiting — a very common mistake at this level.

The knight to c6 is a touch odd because it invites d5. But d5 isn't as good as it looks — it blocks the very bishop we just developed, and pushing the pawn weakens a square the knight can hop into on e5. Better to just keep developing.
teaches: do not push into your own bishop

moves.spoken: So the knight comes to f3. Note that a bishop sortie to g4 here would be a blunder — the sacrifice on f7 with check refutes it, and it must be that capture first, not the knight jump, which only draws.
So we crash on f7 with check. The king loses castling rights and the whole kingside is wrecked — well worth it, even though the d4-pawn will hang at the very end, so this isn't the usual clean win.
The knight comes to g5 with check, driving the exposed king.

Queen and knight are the strongest attacking tandem in chess, so the usual 'let the queen support from behind' rule bends here. The queen to e6 is the move — it eyes a landing on f7. We even allow the knight to grab d4 with tempo; it doesn't matter, the queen is going to f7 regardless.

After the king runs to d7, Black threatens to grab on c2. Do we bend over backwards to defend it? Absolutely not — the cleanest, most elegant move is to castle, straight out of the fork, preparing the rook to d1. The c2-grab then simply loses to a rook check on d1 with a skewer. When you do play the rook to d1, watch the weak back rank for discoveries, but the knight-to-e2 check is harmless — the king steps to f1, hitting the queen, and it's over. And when converting, keep completing development — the Russian-school habit of bringing every piece in, even when you're up a queen — then the back-rank mating net with the bishop on b6 finishes it.
A limitation of the speedrun is that these games get won straight out of the opening — but genuinely, every move here was natural, nothing exotic.

The proper way to handle Black's setup is b5 — the a6-and-b5 idea is legitimate, not as bad as its reputation. Karpov famously lost a classical game to Tony Miles from this very opening; White is clearly better, but proving a huge advantage isn't so easy.
